lessonRef.title: Guided practice: automating saving and paying yourself first

focus: automating saving and paying yourself first
objective: Compute a year of saving under an automatic transfer against a year of saving the monthly remainder, and quantify the gap the ordering of the two decisions creates.
scenario: The simulated pay, expenses, and transfer below are invented for this exercise. No real household budget is described and none is requested.
safetyNotes: Every figure, person, employer, institution, offer, account, and document on this task sheet is fictional and exists only for practice.
No real transaction is part of this lesson, and no real bank, card, brokerage, tax, or login detail is ever requested. If a task sheet ever appears to ask for one, stop and tell a trusted adult.
This lesson teaches general financial concepts and does not advise anyone about their own money. For a real decision, talk with a trusted adult or a qualified licensed professional.
materials: the fictional pay and expense figures in these directions

tasks.directions: A fictional worker takes home $1,840 a month. Under the first plan, 12% of take-home moves to savings automatically on payday, before any spending. Under the second plan, nothing is transferred and whatever remains at the end of the month is saved. The worker’s spending settles at $1,690 a month under the second plan.

prompts.text: Under the automatic plan, how much moves to savings each month?
What does the automatic plan save over twelve months?
Under the second plan, how much is left at the end of a month?

tasks.directions: Now compare the two plans over a year, and measure the automatic plan against a stated goal.

prompts.text: What does the second plan save over twelve months?
How much more does the automatic plan save over the year?
After 13 months of automatic transfers, how much has the worker saved?
The worker is saving towards a $3,000 goal. How far short is the balance after those 13 months?

The worker earns the same amount under both plans, yet one saves $849.60 more. Explain where that difference comes from, and name one condition under which the automatic plan would fail rather than help.

remediation: Use the fictional scenario and work one graded prompt at a time. For each number response, copy the given fictional quantities into integer cents, choose the operation the wording calls for, calculate, and check the result with an inverse operation or estimate. For each written response, make a claim and support it with at least one detail from the fictional scenario. Use these steps to check the method while keeping every final result in your own response.
extension: Find the transfer percentage that would reach the $3,000 goal in exactly 12 months, and say what monthly spending that would leave.
